I remember small sounds, like water moving through dark stones.
A window holds the afternoon, warm and pale, almost gone.
Somewhere beyond the street, a bird repeats one bright question.
I think about doors left open and words left unsaid.
The clock speaks softly, counting what nobody seems to own.
Dust drifts through sunlight, carrying tiny lost pieces of day.
My hands rest here, calm, forgetting what they almost touched.
Outside, rain considers falling, then decides to wait a while.
Inside, the chair remembers someone sitting, breathing, waiting, becoming still.
A page turns itself, whispering stories no one asked for.
The coffee cup holds brown silence, gentle, bitter, and warm.
I hear a distant train, pulling something heavy toward elsewhere.
Maybe clouds are maps for people who never leave home.
The floor creaks, remembering footsteps from houses long gone now.
I wonder whether shadows feel tired when evening finally arrives.
The mirror keeps no secrets, only silver, glass, and light.
A forgotten coat hangs there, dreaming of cold and shoulders.
The sky turns purple, like bruised fruit after a storm.
I try to name the hour, but it slips away.
Each breath enters slowly, then leaves like a small tide.
The city hums beneath my thoughts, vast, indifferent, and bright.
A moth circles the lamp, worshiping a false little sun.
I want to keep this minute, folded and safe forever.
The refrigerator murmurs, keeping food cold and secrets mildly hidden.
Leaves scratch at pavement, writing sentences only autumn can read.
There is peace in ordinary things, especially when nobody watches.
I imagine all lost objects meeting in a quiet room.
Keys, coins, buttons, letters, socks, all waiting without complaint there.
The moon appears early, pale as a thumbprint on glass.
Someday maybe I will understand why some songs feel blue.
A child laughs somewhere, and the evening becomes less heavy.
The scent of bread wanders through the kitchen like hope.
I watch my reflection blink, wondering which of us remembers.
The hallway stretches forward, patient, leading nowhere and everywhere together.

A book lies open, holding a place for someone absent.

I fold paper into wings, but it refuses to fly.

Perhaps time is not a line but a slow circle.
I keep returning to the same thought, like a bee.
The kettle sighs, ready to pour warmth into waiting cups.
Morning will come again, pale and ordinary, asking to begin.
I will make tea and pretend the world is manageable.
The spoon will stir, making small whirlpools in brown water.
The cup will warm my palms, and that is enough.
Beyond the glass, the street will shine with slow cars.
A neighbor will cough, and the day will become real.
I will hear the elevator stop, then doors sliding open.
Someone will speak, and sound will break the quiet carefully.
I will answer, or maybe not, letting silence remain there.
The phone will glow, holding messages from people far away.
I will read words, feeling strange intimacy through cold glass.
Some messages are seeds, some are stones, some are mirrors.
I will choose one and carry it like a coin.
Later I might forget why it felt so important then.
The afternoon will arrive with dust and gold in air.
Birds will argue on the wire, small, black, and alive.
The wind will turn pages no one bothered to mark.
I will sit among these things, neither sad nor happy.
Maybe that is the point: to remain, to notice, enough.
The evening will collect colors, then fold them into darkness.
I will hear my own breathing, a soft private ocean.
Sleep will approach, wearing the face of familiar forgotten rooms.
Dreams will open doors, and I will walk through them.
There I will meet people made from memory and weather.
Some will speak, others will only watch with gentle eyes.
One will hand me a key that fits no lock.
I will hold it anyway, grateful for weight and cold.
Awake again, I will find sunrise pressing against the curtain.
The day will ask me to become useful once more.
I will wash my face and practice being a person.
The mirror will show a stranger who knows my name.
I will nod to him, or her, or perhaps them.
Breakfast will be simple, because complicated mornings require too much.
Bread, butter, silence, and the small courage to begin again.
The kettle will sing its thin song, and I listen.
Outside, a truck will pass, carrying things toward unknown owners.
I will imagine each object landing softly in someone's hands.
Maybe someone needs the thing I cannot see this morning.
The world is full of invisible errands, secret deliveries, hope.
I will put on shoes, preparing for my own errand.
The door will open, and the hallway will smell familiar.
Elevator buttons will glow, each one a possible destination today.
I will press one, and steel doors will close gently.
Downstairs, the lobby will hold its cool, empty, waiting stillness.
The street will be loud, but I will move carefully.
Traffic lights will change, giving everyone little pieces of time.
A bus will breathe and kneel, letting passengers enter slowly.
I will walk past coffee, laundry, flowers, and closed shutters.
Each shop will seem like a sleeping animal, breathing softly.
At last I will arrive, wherever here becomes, and begin.
